finding: Five latent genomic factors across 14 disorders explain ~66% of genetic variance on average; extensive pleiotropy and limited disorder-specific signal in key factors.
Replicated neurobiological findings exist for p, externalizing, thought disorder, internalizing, distress, and depression dimensions, with important maturity limitations.
p is reproducible across statistical representations, but its substantive meaning requires criterion validation and should not be treated as disease ontology.
General psychiatric genetic liability often predicts symptoms as well as disorder-specific PGS, but residual disorder-specific signal remains.
Shared psychosis, schizophrenia-predominant and bipolar-predominant components can be separated.
Schizoaffective disorder has lower interrater reliability than schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and unipolar depression.
General plus positive, negative, disorganized, manic and depressive psychosis dimensions cut across diagnoses and predict biotypes.
Two cortical/subcortical psychosis subtypes span schizophrenia-spectrum and psychotic bipolar disorder.
Family genetic risk and environmental exposures independently contribute to schizophrenia and bipolar risk with partially different weights.
GAD, MDD and PTSD share a strong internalizing factor; 38% of MDD genetic signals were disorder-specific.
Major anxiety disorders share substantial genetic liability; threat-response biology is broad rather than disorder-exclusive.
Fear and GAD show high genetic correlation with partial fear-distress differentiation.
Transdiagnostic CBT is effective for depression/anxiety and often comparable to disorder-specific CBT.
ASD and ADHD have shared loci plus differentiating loci with opposite effect directions.
ASD-specific genetic pathways remain after removing shared ADHD liability.
Genetic contribution among diagnosed ASD/ADHD cases changed by diagnosis year, consistent with boundary broadening.
Rare pathogenic variants and common polygenic liability contribute partly independently to pediatric ADHD.
Tourette/OCD/ADHD symptoms form heritable cross-disorder symmetry and disinhibition phenotypes.
OCD has robust own loci but shares genetic risk with anxiety, depression, anorexia and Tourette.
OCRDs fit separable compulsivity and grooming dimensions.
Eating disorders and OCD show correlated cortical/striatal transcriptomic effects despite disorder-specific differences.
Anorexia has strong metabolic genetic architecture that is not reducible to compulsivity.
Obsessive-compulsive symptoms genetically correlate strongly with OCD, supporting an OCS continuum.
Large replicated externalizing factor with broad neural architecture supports disinhibition as a transdiagnostic liability.
SUDs share strong externalizing liability but also internalizing and substance-specific genetic effects.
Addiction risk contains broad externalizing and substance-specific pathways.
BPD has heritable disorder signal but strongest correlations span PTSD, depression, ADHD, antisocial behavior, and self-harm.
Disinhibited and antagonistic externalizing spectra are supported across SUD and personality pathology.
Confirmed autoimmune psychosis was rare (~0.3%) in broad psychiatric services; targeted high-risk testing identified immunotherapy-responsive cases.
Autoimmune encephalitis was confirmed in a selected tertiary FEP cohort, showing context-dependent yield.
Phenotype-guided serum/CSF testing and confirmatory methods are required; positive serum alone can mislead.
Substance-induced psychosis has substantial but incomplete transition to schizophrenia-spectrum illness.
Medical causes of FEP include neurologic, infectious, autoimmune, metabolic and drug-related diseases; workup should be guided by history/exam/routine tests/red flags.
